To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interaction between beta and gamma oscillations in the basal ganglion is a feature of intact rat globus pallidum and is differentially modulated by dopamine acting on D1 and D1 receptors, which is consistent with the hypothesis that dopamine acts on direct and indirect pathways.

(1) beta and gamma oscillations in GP are negatively correlated, (2) these fluctuations are nested within delta oscillations in GP, (3) this nesting is different for gamma and beta, (4) dopamine D1 and dopamine D2 receptors modulate this nesting in opposite ways.

the interaction of beta and gamma frequencies in basal ganglia is a feature of the intact brain and that dopamine D1/D2 receptors have opposing roles in the maintenance of this interaction and in the organization of LFP frequency bands in the basal gangliain intact rats.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the basal ganglia are hierarchically organized and that dopamine plays a critical role in the maintenance of this organization.

dopamine is a critical regulator of the hierarchical organization and balance of frequency bands in basal ganglia, and this may be important in normal basal ganglia functioning and in basal ganglia diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interaction between beta and gamma frequencies in basal ganglia is not a pathology specific to Parkinson's disease but a fundamental feature of normal brain activity.
the basal ganglia has a complex and organized pattern of oscillatory activity, and that dopamine has a key role in regulating these oscillatory patterns.
